record.paper_title: Open Problems in Engineering and Quality Assurance of Safety Critical Machine Learning Systems
record.original_question: How can requirements for a safety-critical subsystem that contains machine-learning models be rigorously broken down into machine-learning-model requirements while combining deductive engineering with inductive machine-learning development and using safety-analysis approaches such as black-box verification, rule-based safeguarding, redundant and diverse architectures, and modification patterns that avoid the 'Change Anything Change Everything' principle?

evidence.quote: In fact, a subsystem should be subdivided and verified based on its development process, combining the conventional deductive approach with the inductive approach that is unique to machine learning [14]. Rigorous breakdown of subsystem requirements into machine-learning model requirements is essential for safety-critical machine-learning systems. In this process, safety analysis methods and processes are important, such as: black box verification; encapsulation of machine-learning models by rule-based safeguarding; redundant & diverse architecture that mitigates and absorbs the uncertainty of machine learning models; system modification patterns to cope with additional requirements without modification of the machine-learning model, in order to avoid the principle of CACE as much as possible.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a safety-critical system S that is decomposed into subsystems, some of which contain one or more machine-learning (ML) models. Classical (deductive) engineering produces components whose behavior is specified and verified against explicit requirements, while ML components are obtained inductively from data and therefore carry residual uncertainty. Suppose S has a set of system-level safety requirements R_S. For each subsystem U ⊆ S that contains ML models M_1, ..., M_k, one wishes to derive a set of ML-model-level requirements R_{M_i} such that:

(i) Satisfaction of R_{M_1}, ..., R_{M_k}, together with the requirements assigned to the non-ML parts of U, formally entails the subsystem-level requirements R_U allocated from R_S.
(ii) The derivation simultaneously accommodates the deductive development process used for non-ML components and the inductive development process used for the ML models.
(iii) The derivation is compatible with, and exploits, the following safety-analysis mechanisms: (a) black-box verification of trained ML models; (b) encapsulation of ML models by rule-based safeguards that constrain their outputs; (c) redundant and diverse architectures that mitigate and absorb the uncertainty of ML models; (d) system-modification patterns that allow new requirements to be satisfied without retraining or altering the ML model, so as to limit the "Change Anything Change Everything" (CACE) effect by which any change to an ML model can affect any of its outputs.

Provide a rigorous methodology — i.e., a formal framework, a set of decomposition rules, and an associated proof obligation discharge procedure — for performing the breakdown R_U ↦ {R_{M_i}} satisfying (i)–(iii), and demonstrate its soundness.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature on safety assurance of ML-based systems (assurance cases, ISO 21448/SOTIF, ISO/PAS 8800, AMLAS, and surveys on ML safety) continues to treat rigorous decomposition of system-level safety requirements into ML-model-level requirements as an open engineering and methodological challenge. No general, formally validated methodology that simultaneously combines deductive/inductive development and the listed safety-analysis mechanisms (black-box verification, rule-based safeguarding, redundant/diverse architectures, CACE-avoiding modification patterns) appears to have been established.

status_evidence.title: Guidance on the Assurance of Machine Learning in Autonomous Systems (AMLAS)
status_evidence.snippet: AMLAS provides a process for systematically integrating safety assurance into the development of ML components, framing requirements decomposition as an ongoing area of methodological development.
status_evidence.claim: Decomposing system safety requirements into ML-component requirements remains an active methodological problem.

status_evidence.title: ISO/PAS 8800 — Road vehicles: Safety and artificial intelligence
status_evidence.snippet: Standardization effort (in progress) addressing AI safety in road vehicles, including allocation of safety requirements to ML components.
status_evidence.claim: Industry standards are still being drafted, indicating no settled rigorous decomposition methodology.
